newsitem.title: USA: Stunned traders try to explain wheat seeding data.
newsitem.headline: Stunned traders try to explain wheat seeding data.

text.p: What happened to all the U.S. winter wheat acreage?
This was the question confronting the grain industry Friday morning as it struggled to figure out why winter wheat seedings for the 1997 crop were pegged at their lowest level since 1978.

The U.S. Department of Agriculture estimated winter wheat seedings for the 1997 crop at 48.22 million acres, well below the average projection in a Reuter analysts survey of 51.40 million. Hard red winter wheat seedings were estimated at 34.1 million acres, down five percent from last year.
The USDA's estimate for soft red winter wheat seedings was down sharply at just less than 10 million acres, off 15 percent from last year.
"The winter wheat number's a shocker," one floor broker at the Kansas City Board of Trade said. "Suddenly the ball's back in their (the wheat producers') court."
"They must have missed some of their survey area or added wrong," one Oklahoma dealer said. "This is absurdly low."
Many dealers noted with irony that fall planting conditions had been mostly favorable for hard red winter wheat.
The central U.S. Plains received timely rains in September and October, and with the exception of some areas of Kansas, fields were never too wet to prevent work.

Traders speculated that part of the reason for the low seedings estimate stemmed from last year's drought in the High Plains, which caused many farmers to abandon their hard red winter wheat crop and plant grain sorghum in the late spring.

Mark Hodges, executive director of the Oklahoma Wheat Commission, said it was likely that producers in the southern Plains may not have been able to harvest their sorghum early enough. This, then, would have delayed wheat seedings.
"In the southern Great Plains and speaking strictly about hard red winter wheat, I'd say that's the reason we're down five percent (from last year)," Hodges said.
Meanwhile, the USDA blamed rains for the estimated decline in soft red winter wheat acreage.

"Unlike last year, rainy weather has persisted through the fall, preventing planting on thousands of acres directly, or, in slowing row harvest to the point that many acres did not get in from the (Mississippi) Delta up through northwest Ohio," the USDA said on Friday in its state-by-state breakdown of wheat seedings.

One grain dealer in south central Kansas also speculated that many soft red winter wheat producers were planning to raise new genetically-altered crops like Monsanto's Roundup Ready soybeans next spring, and had set aside wheat acreage for this purpose.
